text:
Short answer: no. If anything, the panel's composition is the weakest thread you could pull.

The logic doesn't work in your favour. You're a woman, the successful candidate is a woman, and everyone deciding was a woman. There's no configuration of gender bias there that disadvantages you specifically. An all-women panel in a bank's risk function is somewhat unusual statistically, but "unusual" and "evidence of unfairness toward me" are different claims, and only the second one would matter. If you raise it, you'll sound like you're reaching, and that will colour how the rest of your concerns are read — including the legitimate ones.

There's also a practical cost. Panel composition is the kind of thing that feels significant when you're disappointed and looking for an explanation, and it can quietly become the organising story you tell yourself about what happened. That tends to crowd out the more useful question, which is whether the role was actually scoped the way you assumed.

On that: it's worth sitting with the possibility that the decision was defensible. Head of risk modelling at a bank is often much less about modelling depth than the title implies. A large share of the job can be supervisory dialogue, model governance, IRB or stress-testing approvals, documentation that survives regulatory review, and managing a team of people who do the technical work. "Broad experience of regulatory affairs" may not be a euphemism for a weaker candidate — it may be the thing they actually needed most, and a master's in finance plus deep regulatory exposure is a coherent profile for that. Your PhD and nine years are strong, but they're strong on the axis you'd naturally weight highest, which isn't necessarily theirs. Go back and reread the job description and person specification. If regulatory experience was listed as essential and weighted heavily, you have your answer.

The thing that genuinely warrants attention is the silence. Two weeks without a response to a direct request for written reasons is poor practice regardless of the outcome, and it's the one concrete fact you have.

I'd send a short, unemotional follow-up: reference your original request and its date, ask again for written feedback against the published selection criteria, and ask who owns the request if it isn't the person you wrote to. Copy HR if you originally wrote only to the hiring manager. Keep it to a few lines and keep any hint of grievance out of it — you may want a relationship with this organisation later.

If that produces nothing, or produces something that doesn't match the published criteria, that's the point at which it's worth looking into what your jurisdiction entitles you to. Rules on written reasons for recruitment decisions vary a lot, so it's worth checking locally rather than assuming.
